claim: SQLite's 64-bit integer storage spans -9223372036854775808 through +9223372036854775807, and integers within that range are exact.
quote: This gives a storage range of -9223372036854775808 to +9223372036854775807, inclusive. Integers within this range are exact.

claim: Because SQLite's binary-64 REAL cannot exactly represent most decimal fractions, a forced-REAL decimal addition such as 0.1 + 0.2 is subject to approximation rather than exact decimal arithmetic.
quote: Not every decimal number with fewer than 16 significant digits can be represented exactly as a binary-64 number. In fact, most decimal numbers with digits to the right of the decimal point lack an exact binary-64 equivalent.

claim: In PostgreSQL, numeric precision counts significant digits on both sides of the decimal point, while scale counts only fractional digits to the right of it.
quote: The precision of a numeric is the total count of significant digits in the whole number, that is, the number of digits to both sides of the decimal point. The scale of a numeric is the count of decimal digits in the fractional part, to the right of the decimal point.

claim: PostgreSQL rounds a numeric value that has more fractional digits than the declared scale, then raises an error if its integer digits exceed precision minus scale.
quote: If the scale of a value to be stored is greater than the declared scale of the column, the system will round the value to the specified number of fractional digits. Then, if the number of digits to the left of the decimal point exceeds the declared precision minus the declared scale, an error is raised.

locator: §3 Type Affinity; §3.1.1 Affinity Name Examples (DECIMAL(10,5) maps to NUMERIC by rule 5)
claim: SQLite assigns a DECIMAL declaration NUMERIC affinity, and a NUMERIC-affinity column may hold values from all five storage classes, so the declaration does not by itself force exact fixed-scale decimal storage.
quote: A column with NUMERIC affinity may contain values using all five storage classes.

claim: SQLite's documentation states that in a binary-64 column holding dollars and cents, only .00, .25, .50, and .75 cent values are exact, while other fractional amounts are approximations.
quote: For example, if you have a database column that is intended to hold an item price in dollars and cents, the only cents value that can be exactly represented are 0.00, 0.25, 0.50, and 0.75. Any other numbers to the right of the decimal point result in an approximation.

claim: SQLite performs integer arithmetic on two integer operands only when no overflow would result; if integer arithmetic would overflow, it uses IEEE 754 floating-point arithmetic instead.
quote: The other arithmetic operators perform integer arithmetic if both operands are integers and no overflow would result, or floating point arithmetic, per IEEE Standard 754, if either operand is a real value or integer arithmetic would produce an overflow.

claim: PostgreSQL's bigint addition checks for signed 64-bit overflow and raises the error "bigint out of range" instead of promoting the result to floating point.
SQLite's TEXT-to-INTEGER cast takes the longest prefix that forms an integer and ignores the rest, so '12x' converts to 12 rather than failing.
quote: When casting a TEXT value to INTEGER, the longest possible prefix of the value that can be interpreted as an integer number is extracted from the TEXT value and the remainder ignored. Any leading spaces in the TEXT value when converting from TEXT to INTEGER are ignored.

claim: PostgreSQL's integer input parser allows trailing whitespace but treats any other trailing character as invalid syntax, so an input such as '12x' fails instead of converting.
PostgreSQL recommends its exact numeric type for monetary amounts and says numeric addition, subtraction, and multiplication yield exact results where possible.
quote: The type numeric can store numbers with a very large number of digits. It is especially recommended for storing monetary amounts and other quantities where exactness is required. Calculations with numeric values yield exact results where possible, e.g., addition, subtraction, multiplication.

claim: PostgreSQL initially types a numeric constant that contains a decimal point or exponent as numeric, not as binary floating point.
quote: Constants that contain decimal points and/or exponents are always initially presumed to be type numeric.
